newsitem.title: USA: Clinton triumphant, Republicans cling to Congress.
newsitem.headline: Clinton triumphant, Republicans cling to Congress.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Wednesday basked in the glow of a big re-election victory, but his joy was tempered at the prospect of political battles with Republicans who clung to control of Congress.

"I am more grateful than I can say. You have given me an opportunity and a responsibility that comes to few people. I will do my best," Clinton told cheering supporters in his home town of Little Rock, Arkansas, after soundly defeating Republican challenger Bob Dole to become the first Democrat re-elected to the White House since Franklin Roosevelt in 1944.
Clinton was scheduled to return to Washington later on Wednesday to focus on personnel changes for his second term before leaving for an Asian tour next week.
He won most of the big states in Tuesday's election and piled up 379 Electoral College votes to 159 for Dole. The winner needed 270.

It was a particularly sweet triumph for the 50-year-old Clinton because he was written off as politically irrelevant two years ago when, in a mid-term election seen as a referendum on his presidency, Republicans seized control of Congress from his Democrats.

But partisan battles between the White House and Capitol Hill, including investigations into alleged Clinton administration ethical abuses, were guaranteed as Republicans easily held on to the Senate in Tuesday's election and were headed for another majority, though reduced, in the House of Representatives.
In his victory statement, Clinton appealed for an end to partisanship, saying "it is time to put country ahead of party."
"They (the voters) are sending us a message -- work together, meet our challenges, put aside the politics of division and build America's community together," he said.

Dole, 73, the former Senate majority leader from Kansas, conceded defeat with aplomb. "It hurts to lose an election, but stay involved and keep fighting the good fight," Dole told supporters at a Washington hotel.
The Democrats fell short of the 19 seats they needed to seize control of the 435-seat House. However, the reduced Republican majority could give moderates more influence.
House Speaker Newt Gingrich, who is certain to remain in the job despite being blamed for creating the conditions that led to Clinton's revival, pledged to reach out to Clinton.

"I think we ought to work with him, give him a chance to lead in the direction he campaigned on. And if he sticks with the things he campaigned on we should to be able to find some common ground to actually pass some things that are good for America early in 1997," he said.
With 97 percent of election precincts reporting, Clinton had 50 percent of the vote to 41 percent for Dole and nine percent for the Reform Party candidate, Ross Perot.

Clinton aides were quick to claim that the president -- denigrated by Republicans for having won in 1992 with only 43 percent of the vote -- had won a strong mandate for governing by receiving about 50 percent of the vote.
"I think the President feels that he's got a very strong mandate from the American people to complete his agenda," White House Chief of Staff Leon Panetta told CNN.
"The American people want action. They don't want insults, they don't want gridlock, they don't want partisanship, they want action," he said.
Computerized voter tallies by the networks projected Clinton the winner in 31 of the 50 U.S. states plus the District of Columbia, to 19 states for Dole.
Television networks said fewer than 50 percent of eligible voters cast their ballots, a record low turnout. The previous lowest turnout in a presidential election was 50.1 percent in 1988.
Winning Congress for a second consecutive term for the first time in 68 years, Republicans will keep control of the congressional committees investigating alleged Clinton administration wrongdoing.
They made clear they would pursue inquiries into the president's political, business and personal affairs, including recent revelations on campaign fundraising from foreign interests.
Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott of Mississippi said voters were sending a Republican Congress back to keep Clinton under political lock and key.
In an NBC interview, Lott suggested the campaign finance scandal would be the subject of hearings in the Senate Commerce Committee and possibly by an independent counsel.
The key to Clinton's victory appeared clearly to be that voters rated personal security and national prosperity far above character issues and tax-cut promises pushed by Dole.

To Republican threats of more investigations, Panetta said: "If there's anything that was rejected last night by the American people, it was the personal attacks that were made against the president, not only by Bob Dole but by Ross Perot."

The Republicans kept the Senate by winning open seats previously held by Democrats in Alabama, Nebraska and Arkansas. They expanded their majority in the 100-seat chamber by at least one seat to 54-45 with one race in Oregon still undecided.
